title: ayam atma brahma — a week each
hook: why would a teacher describe the self only by what it isn't?
carry: ayam atma brahma — a week each
tomorrow: Om has three sounds. so what's the fourth part?

segments.voice: Yesterday, ayam atma brahma spoke in the first person: I am this, and the one who knows it as wide as the world. Today the same text describes that self by turning down every answer.

A friend asks what the new place in town is like, and the only answer anyone has is: not a café, not a bar, not really a bookstore either. As descriptions go, it's close to useless. The Brihadaranyaka uses that exact move, on purpose, for the biggest thing it talks about. Asked about the self, Yajnavalkya answers King Janaka with two words, twice: neti neti. Not this, not this. So why would a teacher describe something only by what it isn't?
screen: `NOT A CAFÉ, NOT A BAR.` → `NETI NETI: NOT THIS, NOT THIS.` → `WHY ONLY WHAT IT ISN'T?`

segments.voice: Here's the passage, in plain words. This great unborn self lives in the space within the heart, ruler of all, lord of all. It doesn't grow greater by good deeds, or smaller by bad ones. This self is not this, not this. It can't be grasped, so it isn't grasped. It can't be broken, so it doesn't break. It doesn't cling, so it isn't bound. It doesn't tremble, and it isn't harmed. Now the puzzle starts to solve itself. Anything that can be pointed at, a thought, a feeling, a body, a role, is something the self can see. Whatever can be seen gets set aside: not this. The refusal isn't emptiness. It keeps the self from being mistaken for one more item on the list. There's a second puzzle nearby. Earlier in the same chapter, the text said: as one acts, so one becomes. So do deeds matter or not? The text joins the two itself. Deeds shape the person who wants; the self beneath, it says, doesn't grow by deeds or shrink. And the one who knows it, the next verse says, becomes calm, patient, collected, and sees the self in everything.
screen: `UNGRASPABLE, UNBREAKABLE, UNBOUND.` · `WHATEVER CAN BE SEEN: NOT THIS.` · `AS ONE ACTS, SO ONE BECOMES.` · then, large: `CALM, AND THE SELF IN ALL.`

segments.voice: Pick one object within reach, a cup, a pen, your own hand, and name it silently. Then notice that you're the one seeing it, and set it aside: not this. Do the same with whatever shows up next, a sound, a thought, and keep resting as the one who sees.
Ayam atma brahma, met through the back door: neti neti, not this, not this. The self, described by setting aside everything that can be pointed at.
Hold on to it: ayam atma brahma — a week each; not this, not this, and still, the self. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: Advaita teachers often use 'neti neti' as a method of inquiry: setting aside body, mind and role one by one as things seen, to point at the self that sees.

guess: this self is Brahman, known by setting aside what it isn't
a vow to refuse every pleasure and every comfort
a teaching that the self is the body alone

fork.setup: a friend says: if the self isn't changed by good or bad deeds, why bother being good? what does this chapter actually hold?
options: it agrees: the self is untouched, so deeds don't really matter.
both: deeds shape the one who wants; the self beneath isn't changed.
only ritual deeds count; ordinary choices leave no mark.
fork.reveal: the chapter says as one acts, so one becomes, and also that the self doesn't grow or shrink by deeds. the knower, it adds, becomes calm and patient.

original.note: Sanskrit: not so, not so; read as 'not this, not this' (Brihadaranyaka 4.4.22).

trapdoor: what you thought: a description that gives up.
what it means: a way of setting aside whatever can be pointed at, so the self isn't mistaken for an object.
what a scholar hears: Brihadaranyaka 4.4.22 pairs neti neti with ungraspable, unbreakable, unbound; 4.4.5 in the same chapter says as one acts, so one becomes.

chat.says: covering nani's kids class. her notes on the self just say 'neti neti' 😐 how do i teach that?
options: let them name things they can see, then ask: who's seeing? not this, not this.

skip it; the text never says what the self is, so there's nothing to teach.
chat.meaning: Neti neti sets aside whatever can be pointed at, so the self isn't mistaken for one more thing. It isn't a claim of nothingness.

neti neti.meaning: not this, not this: the self described by what it isn't

Yajnavalkya.meaning: the sage who teaches King Janaka about the self

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4.22 (this great unborn self, in the space within the heart, ruler of all, lord of all; not greater by good deeds, not less by bad; not this, not this; ungraspable, unbreakable, unattached, unbound, it does not tremble, it is not harmed)

Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4.23 (the eternal greatness of the knower of Brahman does not grow by deeds or shrink; calm, restrained, withdrawn, patient, collected, he sees the self in the self and sees all as the self)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4.5–6 (as one acts, so one becomes; so much for the one who desires; the one without desire, being Brahman, goes to Brahman)

notes: Block 'ayam atma brahma — a week each', day 6 of 8 (1761–1768).

Neti neti also appears at Brihadaranyaka 2.3.6 and 3.9.26; here it is taken from 4.4.22. The reading 'whatever can be seen is set aside' is the Advaita use of the phrase; other schools read it as denying limits to Brahman rather than as a method of inquiry. Confirm the framing is fair.
Day 1762 already taught 4.4.5 ('as one acts, so one becomes'); here it is only recalled as the second half of the puzzle.
Puzzle shape (v3): the odd detail is a description made only of refusals. Priya preps Nani's Sunday class from her notes.
